question: One start-up aims for 1% of a $100 billion market, another to dominate a tiny one. Which plan does Peter Thiel prefer?
options: A slice of the huge market
answer: All of the tiny market. Thiel calls talk of ‘1% of a $100 billion market’ a red flag: a huge market either has no good place to start or is full of rivals. A small, close-knit one can be served better than anyone else does, then widened. Facebook began with just Harvard’s students.
move: Judge a market by the share you can own, not by its size.
trap: ‘A slice of the huge market’: 1% of a lot sounds like a lot.
simply: It’s easier to be the best chess player in your class than the thousandth best in the world. Win your class first; then the school; then the town.
why: The same choice comes up for a shop, a freelancer or a new club: aim at everyone and compete with everyone, or become the obvious choice for a few. Being first choice somewhere small often beats being one option among hundreds somewhere big.
reference: Peter Thiel with Blake Masters, Zero to One: Notes on Startups, or How to Build the Future (Crown Business, 2014), ch. 5, Last Mover Advantage
